title: A practical guide to QBR metrics for support teams | Pylon
summary: Learn which QBR metrics for support teams matter most, how to track them by account, and how to turn quarterly trends into clear next actions.
body_markdown:
A fast response time can look like good news during an account’s quarterly review. But if your customers keep asking about the same unresolved problem, that number tells only part of the story.


Quarterly business review (QBR) metrics for support teams bring those details together. By looking at all of the team’s metrics as part of a bigger picture, you can see what improved for each account and agree on what still needs work before renewal.


## What are QBR metrics for support teams?


CSAT survey view from Pylon


QBR metrics measure support performance in the context of each customer’s goals. They cover how quickly you respond, whether problems stay resolved, and how customers feel about the help they get.


By definition, QBRs are a quarterly business review. Often, they’re structured like meetings with a customer to assess progress and plan the next quarter. Customer support metrics supply evidence for that conversation.


For example, an account may want to expand their contract and use your software in a new department. Repeated timeouts during bulk exports could delay that expansion, even if you answer every request promptly. Reviewing those problems alongside with the account’s plans helps you identify what needs fixing before the[customer success team](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/customer-success-vs-customer-support) can discuss renewal or an expanded contract.


## Which support metrics should be reviewed each quarter?


Look at the support metrics that tell you if your team can deliver the improvements you promise. Account health metrics, like customer experience and operational efficiency, can reveal if the customer is happy with what you’re already offering, or if there’s room for improvement before they expand.


Use these[customer experience KPIs](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/customer-experience-kpis) as your baseline and choose the measures that explain your account’s main challenges.


Group Metric What to examine


Customer experience[Customer satisfaction score (CSAT)](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/customer-satisfaction-score) Satisfaction with a recent interaction, alongside survey response counts


Customer experience[Customer effort score (CES)](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/customer-effort-score) How easy customers say it was to get help


Customer experience[Net promoter score (NPS)](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/net-promoter-score) Willingness to recommend your company (which reflects the broader relationship, not support alone)


Customer experience[First contact resolution (FCR)](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/customer-service-first-contact-resolution) How many eligible issues are resolved in the first interaction without further contact


Customer experience Reopen rate How often closed issues return, using a defined follow-up window


Operational efficiency First response time (FRT) The wait for a qualifying reply (decide whether AI replies count)


Operational efficiency[Average resolution time](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/time-to-resolution) Time to resolve closed issues, with consistent rules for support hours and pauses


Operational efficiency SLA adherence The share of applicable service-level agreement targets met (separate response and resolution targets)


Operational efficiency QA score Response quality against a consistent review rubric


Follow-through Escalations Issues that need specialist help and how long the handoff takes


Follow-through Recurring issue volume Repeated requests about the same underlying problem


Follow-through Backlog Open issues and their age (note work blocking a customer's plans)


Team capacity Ticket volume vs. headcount Demand relative to available team members, allowing for issue complexity


Agent impact Tickets with substantive agent work Issues where an agent meaningfully contributed, like an accepted draft or investigation


Agent impact Automated resolution vs. team time What agents finish independently and where people still spend their time


Team capacity[Forecasted headcount](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/budget-friendly-support-systems) The people needed for expected demand after accounting for agent work

Keep customer results separate from headcount. Average handle time (AHT), which measures active work on an issue, helps you assess the team time behind ticket totals. ## How to track QBR metrics by account in 5 steps


Consistent definitions and account records make it possible to compare your work every quarter. Start with the following five steps before sitting down with a customer.


### 1. Establish metric definitions before you compare accounts


Before you get started, write down each calculation and its reporting window, so you can repeat it later. Calculate SLA adherence from applicable targets, excluding issues without an SLA. Here’s what that looks like for a few common metrics:


- **FCR.** Divide eligible issues resolved on first contact by all eligible issues, then multiply by 100 to get a percentage. Define what counts as another contact so Slack threads and email exchanges follow the same rule.
- **Reopen rate.** Divide the number of issues that reopen within a fixed period by all closed issues in that window, then multiply by 100 for a percentage.
- **Average resolution time.** Divide total counted resolution time by resolved issues and document any excluded hours and work done by an AI agent.


In Pylon, replies from AI Agents count as a first response for SLA purposes. Keep that distinction visible when agent adoption changes between quarters.


### 2. Map every support conversation to the right account


Every conversation from Slack, Teams, and email should be linked to the right account. Check shared consultants or partner contacts carefully, since one person may work with several customers. Otherwise, their requests can distort the account’s results.


### 3. Review account trends in context


Break the account’s issues down by reason for the contact. For the planned department rollout, separate export timeouts from unrelated product questions. Then check whether those export failures recurred, remained open, or repeatedly needed escalations.


That context makes a[customer health score](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/b2b-customer-health-score) easier to understand. A declining score should lead your conversation toward identifying what changed (if anything) and whether the rollout is still blocked.


### 4. Compare paired metrics, not single averages


A quarter-wide average alone won’t show which cases need attention. An account can meet its response SLA while resolution time rises. Pair those measures to expose the difference between getting a reply and getting a fix. If the reopen rate also increases, review whether your team may be closing issues before the customer confirms the solution works.


### 5. Check progress before the quarterly review


Review account trends monthly, so you aren’t surprised by an unresolved problem in the QBR. Customer success team members can ask Pylon’s[Slack Agent for an account summary](https://support.usepylon.com/articles/3096059903-how-does-the-slack-agent-work) in an internal Slack channel, then check on the underlying issues with the support team.


## How to turn QBR metrics into action


Analytics view from Pylon


Present leadership with one customer outcome, the measures that explain it, and a specific decision. For example, a customer interested in a new rollout’s outcome is getting the new department working with reliable data exports. You can pair recurring issue volume with resolution time, and use CSAT as a guardrail so faster closure doesn’t come at the expense of the relationship.


Each missing target needs an action, an owner, and a review date. Your dev team might own the export fix, while customer success confirms that the new department can complete its work. Those responsibilities turn[support issues into success signals](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/workflows-support-tickets-success-signals-retention-2025) across teams.


Configure Pylon’s[Automations](https://www.usepylon.com/ai-agents/automations) to surface the issues relevant to your plan, then have the owner check progress before the next account review. A QBR that customer success teams can act on includes evidence of follow-through, not just a snapshot of the original problem.

## FAQ


### What’s a QBR?


A quarterly business review (QBR) is a meeting with a customer to assess progress toward their goals and agree on next steps four times a year. Support teams contribute evidence about improvements delivered that quarter and problems that are still unresolved.


### How often should support teams review and update QBR metrics?


Review account trends monthly and summarize them quarterly. Update your metric set when customer goals or your support model change, and record definition changes so comparisons stay clear.


### What mistakes should support teams avoid when reporting QBR metrics?


Avoid changing denominators and hiding small survey samples to keep your presentation honest. Showing speed without resolution quality can be misleading, too.


Separate account-level results from team capacity, and explain whether AI replies count toward response time.


### How can support teams choose the right QBR metrics?


Start with the customer’s next goal. Then, choose metrics that reveal what may be an obstacle to that goal, and pair performance measures with feedback that shows whether customers found the support useful.


### How do QBR metrics connect support performance to business outcomes?


QBR metrics show whether support problems threaten or improve an account’s likelihood of contract renewal or expansion. They’re one part of the equation, but you’ll still need to talk to customer success teams and the customer. A correlation between support activity and retention doesn’t prove that support caused the outcome.
